summary: Hot or Not is a web app that answers one question for any area in four fire-prone regions: is this place burning more than usual? It turns NASA FIRMS fire detections into one consistent monthly record from 2000 to today. The challenge is that two NASA sensors count fires differently. VIIRS, with its sharper 375 m pixels, detects 3 to 10 times as many fires as the older MODIS, so simply joining their records makes fires seem to explode in 2012. We studied 908,862 VIIRS fires that MODIS also looked at within 15 minutes, learned how likely MODIS was to see each one, and weight every VIIRS detection by that chance and a regional factor. Tested on years the model never saw (2012-2019), yearly totals land within 2.9 to 11.3% of MODIS. That is 5.6% on average, against 11.4% for a simple ratio. With MODIS retiring and S-NPP's fire data ending on 2 November 2026, the record continues on NOAA-20, within 3% of S-NPP. Draw any area and get a burning calendar and a verdict: HOT, NORMAL or NOT.
details:
What it does
Hot or Not shows how much an area burns, month by month, from 2000 to today, on one consistent scale. Pick one of four demo regions (Nile Delta, California and Nevada, south-east Australia, northern Argentina and the Paraguayan Chaco), draw your own area on the map, or type coordinates. You then see:

  • a verdict for the latest month, HOT, NORMAL or NOT, ranked against the same days in every year since 2003
  • a calendar of every month since 2000, as fire counts or compared with normal
  • every fire detection behind the numbers as a dot on the map, with its satellite, time and fire power, and how much it counts
  • a chart of every year, where a click shows all of that year's fires

The data can be downloaded as CSV. A guided "Tell me the story" tour and a "How it works" page with interactive diagrams explain the method to non-experts, and give scientists the full test results.

How it works

  1. Download: about 13.1 million fire detections from NASA FIRMS (MODIS Collection 6.1 on Terra and Aqua; VIIRS 375 m on S-NPP and NOAA-20), plus NASA CMR overpass records, so we know when each satellite was looking.
  2. Clean: remove duplicates and non-vegetation heat sources such as gas flares, using NASA's labels. For recent unlabelled data, also remove detections near known flares or seen at the same spot on 20 or more days in 90.
  3. Match: from 2012 to 2019, find the 908,862 S-NPP VIIRS fires that Aqua MODIS looked at within 15 minutes, and note whether MODIS saw each one.
  4. Learn: a logistic regression on VIIRS-side features (fire radiative power, pixel size, day or night, land cover, cluster size) predicts how likely MODIS is to see a fire. A coverage factor per region and month adds the looks MODIS had that VIIRS lacks, such as Terra's morning pass.
  5. Weigh and add up: each VIIRS fire counts as its weight, and fires add up per month on a 0.05 degree (about 5 km) grid.
  6. Test: hide two years at a time, predict them, and compare with real MODIS counts. The model ships only if it beats a simple ratio method. It did, in 4 of 4 regions.
  7. Publish: a small database and compressed map tiles that the web app reads.

Benefits and intended impact
Anyone can ask whether a fire season is unusual without remote-sensing expertise: journalists, farm cooperatives, environment and air-quality agencies, researchers, students. The 26-year record stays comparable across sensor changes, which matters now that MODIS is retiring and S-NPP stopped sending fire data. It can show the effect of policies. For example, autumn rice-straw burning in the Nile Delta, the source of Cairo's "black cloud", fell from about 500 detections a year (2003-2016) to about 215 (2017-2025). Every number can be traced to the dots behind it, and the method and its tests are public.

Tools

  • Pipeline: Python 3.12 (standard library only) and SQLite.
  • Web app: Node.js 24 built-ins and plain JavaScript (no framework, no build step), MapLibre GL, Apache ECharts, Terra Draw, the OpenFreeMap basemap, and IBM Plex Sans.
  • Hosting: a Linux VPS with systemd and Caddy.
  • Automated tests check the pipeline and the app.
  • Claude Code (Anthropic's AI coding assistant) helped write and test the code and documentation, under the team's direction.
  • No hardware.

What is creative about it

  • Instead of one fixed ratio, every VIIRS fire gets its own weight, so small fires count less and big ones more, and the correction adapts to place and season.
  • A one-word verdict (HOT, NORMAL, NOT) and a calendar heatmap make 26 years readable at a glance.
  • "How it works" lets readers follow one real day (13 September 2017, Nile Delta) through every step, and watch a gas flare get caught.
  • The dots on the map are the same data as the calendar, so the numbers can be checked.

Factors we considered

  • Honest testing: the model is checked on years it never saw. We report where it is weaker: on 2020-2025, the simple ratio does better, partly because MODIS orbits have drifted.
  • Sensor handovers: S-NPP's fire data ended on 2 November 2026. NOAA-20 carries on, calibrated to agree within 3%.
  • Gas flares versus real fires.
  • Gaps shown as "no data", never as zero, for example the Bolivian and Brazilian parts of the Chaco region.
  • Recent months marked as provisional.
  • Plain language, keyboard access, colour-blind-safe colours, and phone layouts.
  • Current limits: four demo regions. Covering any place on Earth is the next step.
